utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Richterova. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: May I start?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Before we start talking about the document about your appointment to the post of commander, I would like to clarify certain points from your testimony yesterday because we had to finish due to the fact that you were tired. Yesterday you testified about units of the TO and -- or the police that were subordinated to the JNA for operation purposes. What would happen to these units at the end of the operation? Would they stay subordinated to the JNA or would they return to their prior command in the TO or the police?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units that were resubordinated to the JNA for the purposes of accomplishing a certain mission would return into the structure of a TO staff once their mission was accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And would be the case for the police?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same would apply to the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you one more question, but please tell us whether you -- you know it or not because it may go beyond your knowledge. Under the laws in the SAO Krajina, do you know what duties and responsibilities of the minister of the interior were with respect to his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, can you tell us when did you retire from the military, the year?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Are you familiar still with the international laws of war?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, yes, although I've forgotten quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would ask you whether you are familiar with the rule that a commander has a duty to discipline subordinates under his command who commits crime even if, for operational purposes, the subordinate is under somebody else's command. Are you familiar with this rule?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't understood the question. Could you please repeat it? Whether a commander has the duty to punish even his subordinates. Have I understood this correctly?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Let me repeat this question once again. The question was whether the commander has a duty to discipline his subordinate, the -- the person who is under his subordination even if he, for operational purposes, this subordinate is under somebody else command.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I missed your point.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will be more concrete. You have a --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: -- commander of the special police unit, and this commander is -- has a duty to discipline his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This subordinate is put, for operational purposes, under the command of somebody else. And my question is --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: -- whether you are familiar with the rule that in this case the commander of the special police unit - and this is just an example - is still -- has still the duty to discipline his subordinate?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case you mention, if a commander of a special-purpose unit resubordinated his unit -- or rather, allowed his unit to be resubordinated to another commander, then the commander who is now in command of the unit will apply any and all disciplinary matters and will bring the case before a military court, regardless of which unit this member originates from. However, the commander that allowed his unit to be resubordinated does not have the right to then discipline a member of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And this is your understanding of -- of the rules?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you, yourself, ever in the position when you had to discipline a subordinate for having committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A commander does not have the right to punish a soldier who commits a crime. This is the jurisdiction of the military court. A commander can, however, apply disciplinary measures, and that's what I had occasion to do. Criminal -- or rather, prosecution lies within the jurisdiction of a military court. A commander can merely file a criminal report, and then it is up to the court to decide whether this is indeed a crime or not. And then, depending on the outcome, this goes back -- the case goes back to the commander. Of course, this is something that falls within the competence of commanders of all levels, brigades, divisions, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, my question was slightly different. It was only whether you, yourself, was in the position when you had to discipline, not punish, discipline your subordinate.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Have you ever heard the term "Marticevci"?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of the term "Marticevci." Martic's men. This is the police force of the Ministry of the Interior of the SAO Krajina, and they were called in this way. It was a derogatory term, Marticevci, Martic's men, whereas those who sided with Babic were called Babicevci, Babic's men. That is the way they used to call them colloquially out in the streets and then they would point to a person and say: Look, he's a Babicevac, Babic's man, or Marticevac, but in essence it did not really mean anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You say this is the police force of the Ministry of the Interior, and when you say "Babicevci," what do you refer to?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were all the people who did not side with Martic. They term -- call -- styled me a Babicevac, although that wasn't true. They thought that I held his views and supported him in his views and in some of his actions in advocating certain issues. This was a wrong impression, but there it was. It stayed at that. This was even true in Serbia; that's what they thought over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You -- yesterday you referred to a special unit within the police, that this special unit was called the Krajina police. Can you tell us where was this unit based?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This wasn't the Krajina police -- or rather, the Ministry of the Interior of Krajina had its special-purpose unit which intervened in particular cases, on special occasions, and it was stationed in Knin. As for the strength and the composition of the unit, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Any question is: Have you ever heard the term "mopping-up"?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What does this term refer to?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Mopping-up" is not a military term. Again, this would be sweeping of the terrain, but that's a layman's term. Whenever a unit would seize a swath of territory, then the units would be positioned there and the -- the units of the TO or a police unit would follow and sweep the terrain for left-over elements of enemy units to make sure that the entire area is free of enemy forces. So the mopping-up is not really a military term. What we have as an official term is sweeping of an area or -- and sanitisation of an area. This is a Serbo-Croat term which can have more meanings than one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us meanings of these two terms?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You just said the sweeping and the sanitisation.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sweeping of an area, as I just said, means detection of left-over elements of enemy units, their hardware, members of sabotage units, and other asserts with a view to clearing the area of these elements, whereas the sanitisation of an area means to gather up the left-over military hardware, gathering of the wounded and the dead, including animal carcasses, assisting the population, and so on and so forth, with the objective of restoring the area to the condition in which it was prior to the combat activities to the extent possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What would happen to the civilian population in -- in these areas where mopping up or sweeping is undergoing?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of combat activities, before any such combat activities, the population is evacuated to prevent it from getting in harm's way. Once the operation is over, the civilian population is taken back to the area. Those who are left behind either manage to survive or -- or get killed as a result of getting in the cross-fire or in enemy fire or -- or in friendly fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During 1991 do you know if TO or police units were ever assigned to the task of mopping-up during military operations?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was there, the Krajina TO Staff was never given any such task, although, to tell you the truth, we didn't have any units. The same is true for Northern Dalmatia and Lika, although I cannot speak for Banija.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In fact, I was not talking about your staff, your TO Staff, because we already established that you didn't have any units. I was talking about TO units in various zones and police units. This was my question, whether you are aware that they would be assigned to the task of mopping-up the terrain.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This wasn't a task they'd be given, this was their duty; regardless of the scale of the operation, this was something they would do on the orders of the commander of the given operation, although I cannot speak of any specific such case. I am not aware of any.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In the time you were in Krajina, to your knowledge, were there any paramilitary formations operating in the territory?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, to my knowledge, there were not any paramilitary formations that were independent and active in the area. There was one unit belonging to the Serbian Radical Party, but it was in the structure of the 9th Corps. It was part of its organic structure and was not in any way different from the other units that were part of the 9th Corps. All the more so, it was an exemplary unit, as far as I know. I heard that there were paramilitary units involved in the attack in Pakrac [as interpreted], Arkan's men, Giska's men, Captain Dragan's men, and some others whose names I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you are talking about this group which belongs to Serbian Radical Party, where did you -- were they based? Where were they based?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were part of the 121st [as interpreted] or 170th -- or rather, 180th Brigade. I'm not sure which of the two, but they were establishment-wise part of its structure and they were under the command of JNA officers. Ultimately they all came under the 9th Corps, which covered this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And which was this area? What was the name of the area?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A unit was not stationed in one location only; they were near Benkovac, Drnis, and were given their assignments by the 9th Corps. I did not have the opportunity to see the documents issued by the 9th Corps which governed the deployment of the 180th and the 221st Brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, did you see Seselj, Vojislav Seselj, in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What were the circumstances you saw him?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We came to visit the TO staff. I don't know whether was this something that was planned, although probably not because he was not on contract. I don't know Seselj that well. We just chatted about the situation in Krajina in general, whereupon he insisted to be received by Milan Babic. Milan Babic was trying to avoid seeing him, but in the end he did receive him. I don't know what the subject of the discussion was. The then-defence minister, Milan Tarbuk, was with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned that this group belonged to Serbian Radical Party. Do you know who was the leader of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this group?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No. I mean who was generally the leader of this Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leader of the Serbian Radical Party was Professor Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did he ever visit this group in -- which was stationed in Krajina? And we were talking about it a while ago.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He visited his group of soldiers with a group of officers from the 9th Corps. I personally spoke with the commander of the 9th Corps and the commander of the 221st Brigade, Colonel Djukic. I asked about these soldiers, and they had only good things to tell me about them in terms of their conduct, discipline, and so on. For the duration of my stay there, I did not hear anything negative about them. It happened by chance that in the hotel in Knin I came across two men from this group who were resting there, and they were quite content with their position and status within the 9th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were they directly subordinated or incorporated into the JNA, this group of volunteers?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For example, if a battalion had three or four companies, then they constituted one company within that battalion under the command of the battalion commander, and they carried out all orders of the battalion commander. Nobody else issued any orders to them or had anything to do with them, except for the commander of the battalion or commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified in relation to the document 65 ter Exhibit Number 206.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We didn't manage to finish this document, so if -- I would like to ask you to display this document again. Can we scroll down a little bit? Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified, based on this document, that only the General Staff of the JNA had the authority to appoint you to any position. So what happened to this appointment?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday when giving evidence I explained the explanation given by Milan Babic -- or rather, the statement of reasons provided by Milan Babic on the relieving of duties of Mr. Djujic. I told you already that he wasn't happy with Mr. Djujic's work for the reasons I stated. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No. Mr. Maksic, I am today talking about the document when you were appointed to the position of commander. So I want to hear what was your reaction to this appointment.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day I was away on business. I think I travelled to Vrhovina to Korenica. Upon my return to Knin, my associates and colleagues congratulated me, and I knew nothing about the appointment. Nobody had consulted me. I learned of it for the first time on the first channel of Radio Television Belgrade. Milan Babic had no right to do this because I already had a prior appointment within the JNA. Milan Babic wrote this on his own without consulting anybody. I never saw this decision nor signed it. Following this, I immediately informed my commander in Belgrade and chief of the personnel service; they, upon learning of this, considered it to be invalid. After several days I went to Belgrade to explain this in person. Once I returned from Belgrade, I stayed for another couple of days in Knin, and then I received a cable from the General Staff of the JNA to return to Belgrade to resume my prior duties, and that was the end of it. That was the end my command --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- over the TO staff in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know who was later appointed to the position of commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Colonel, or perhaps even, General Milan Torbica was pointed to this post.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have other questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Richterova. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I forgot to ask that I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which -- oh, this document that appoints the --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yeah, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: -- exactly. He read this document yesterday before we adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 128, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Maksic, I am Defence counsel for Mr. Martic. My name is Predrag Milovancevic. We will now begin the part of your examination known as cross-examination. I will be putting questions to you and I would like to receive an answer from you to the extent you know about the things I'm asking you. When providing your biographical data, you stated that you completed all military schools, military academy, and various staff schools. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. You can see that in the documents. You can verify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, when did you enroll into military academy? Do you remember which year, even though I'm sure it was quite a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the military academy based in Belgrade then?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The military academy of land forces is located in a section of Belgrade called Banjica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How long did it last?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I completed military secondary school, I had to study for one year general subjects such as math, chemistry, languages, and so on. And then I had three years of training in the military field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the ethnic make-up of the students attending the military academy. Were they only of one nationality or of different ones?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People attending military academy came from all nationalities and national minorities. There were Albanians, Slovenians, Croats, Hungarians, Slovaks, Ruthenians, Serbs, Romanians. That is to say all communities living at the time in the territory of the former Yugoslavia were represented in the military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time in Yugoslavia, was there an official position and slogan declaring brotherhood and unity among all peoples living in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the main slogan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us during your studies at the military academy, did you see that there was any discrimination among the students based on their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the course of four years of study, there were about 400 of us, I'm not quite sure. A monograph was published with the exact figure of students, but during the four years of my studies there, there was not a single incident that was based on ethnic issues during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, let me warn you about something. Since you and I speak the same language and the interpreters have to translate what we are saying, would you please always make a break after my questions. Please have this in mind. I know that this doesn't come natural, but please try to remember this.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll try to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you said that you completed military academy, and did you acquire any rank following your graduation?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon my graduation I was given a rank of lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Your fellow students who graduated together with you were given an assignment and assigned to various JNA units. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They were assigned throughout the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When the assignment was given specifying who was going to serve where, in which garrison, in which unit, in which institution of the JNA, was the nationality of an officer taken into account?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What schooling did you complete following the military academy?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed command staff school, which was later renamed into higher military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the criterium for admission into this higher military academy? As we have established, there was a regular military academy and the school above it was known as the higher military academy. Was nationality of a student taken into account?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before entering the higher military academy, one had to spend several years serving in the army. Depending on results achieved in the course of service, people were either admitted into the higher military academy or not. Nationality was not taken into account. There were entry exams, and the selection criteria were extremely strict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, how long does the schooling take at the command staff school or higher military academy? How long does it take to complete a course of study?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your schooling at the command staff school, did you observe that any officers were singled out because of their nationality in the sense that some were neglected and some were favoured?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. Just like in the military academy of land forces, there were no such cases. It did not even occur to anyone to raise this. I never heard that there was ever a single incident of this nature. At the time, party units were still quite active and something like this would have been discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You as a JNA officer, did you ever hold any ethnic bias in relation to your fellow officers and students?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, to the contrary. My best friends were officers of different ethnicity, Croats and Macedonians. I can give you their names if that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Upon completing command staff school, you also went to war college?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After command staff school or academy, I served in Sarajevo and then I returned to Belgrade not because I chose so but because I was appointed head of year. Let me explain what this means. Head of year is head of a year of students which normally has 3 to 400 students. After that, I served as commander of a regiment, and then I went to war college.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Which officers are given an opportunity to enroll into war college? What are the criteria?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The criteria first of all entails successful service; that was the most important criterium. And then good grades in schooling. And then the third criterium was the ability to complete the schooling and to command operative and joint units, so that out of 500 to 1.000 applicants, only 10 to 20 are admitted and the decision is made by a special commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your study at this highest school, the war college, did you observe that there were any cases of discrimination on a national basis, that certain officers of a certain ethnic background had privileged status?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I told you about previous schools that I attended applies in this case as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in 1961 you enrolled into military academy, Mr. Maksic, and then you said that in 1985 you were head of year of students attending military academy of land forces in Belgrade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think there was an error a misunderstanding. In 1981 I was head of year, in 1981. I served there for two years in the military academy of land forces, and then for four years I served as a commander of the Belgrade regiment -- Belgrade Corps, 151st Regiment. And then I became head of training section in the department for operations and training within the Belgrade Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As a cadet, you attended the JNA military school. You enrolled there in 1961, and then 20 years later you were head of year again in a military school. In the meantime, did anything change in the attitude of these schools versus the students? So let's say in 1981, was there any difference in terms of the ethnic bias?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The year I attended was the 37th year in succession. There was not a single ethnic-based incident. Vojdanic and Colonel Babic were persons in charge -- Ojdanic and Colonel Babic were in charge of my generation, and there wasn't a single ethnic-based incident that I knew of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Whilst you held the duty of the head of year for the cadets who were in infantry, did you not perform different duties in the Belgrade Corps staff up until 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And these were quite important duties?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was commander of the regiment and head of the training department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your work in this particular time period, after you assumed these commanding duties in mid-1980s up until 1991, did you experience any discrimination among soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, did you hear of and did you know General Spegelj?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the four years I was the commander of the regiment, the Chief of Staff of the first army was General Spegelj, therefore he was my immediate superior and that was, to me, a very high position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you well, General Spegelj was Chief of Staff of the first army stationed in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time I was the commander of the 151st Regiment of the first army because this regiment was part of the 22nd Division and the 22nd Division was part of the 1st Army. This particular regiment was subject to frequent inspections by the army, and two or three times, if not even more, Martin Spegelj would be party to that inspection tour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who was commander of the 1st Army when General Spegelj was Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Gracanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who was commander of the army in Zagreb at the time -- or rather, let's say in 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does the name of General Konrad Kolsek mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to say Kolsek, but I wasn't sure. I know him but that was way back when I was a young officer. He was commander of the 21st Division in the defence of the town of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you watch the movie screened in January 1991 in all the Yugoslav TV stations featuring General Spegelj and Minister Boljkovac who was Croatian minister of police?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. I saw the footage several times, if you're referring to the film which had to do with the organisation and the action of some individuals in the area of Slavonia. I think that the film was shot in Slavonia, if that's the same film you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This particular footage, does it concern the distribution of arms?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And also the killing of officers, their families, wives, and children, if that's the footage you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall some details; others I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that in January 1991 the SFRY Presidency took a decision to disarm all the paramilitary formations in the area of the former Yugoslavia and in -- to bring all the police forces under the legal structure?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the SFRY Presidency passed such a decision. I was involved in its implementation. The defence of the city of Belgrade comprised the largest number of staffs because we had 16 municipalities and 16 TO staffs. I remember that as a matter of urgency, all the weapons and equipment contained in TO depots was supposed to be relocated to JNA depots; in other words, they were to be taken from the jurisdiction of the TOs into the jurisdiction of the JNA. I don't know about this part concerning paramilitary formations. I don't know on which date this was in 1991, whether it was in early 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the SFRY Presidency decision dating from January 1991, but if you're not familiar with that particular one, we will not dwell on it.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time there weren't any armed paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt. It looks like we are keeping up a very fast pace again. If we can remember what you admonished the witness about a little earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We will keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We will have to slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please pause a while before answering my question.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any armed conflict in early March in Pakrac and do you know who took part in it?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the SFRY Presidency session in March 1991 upon -- called upon the proposal of the JNA General Staff to introduce a state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything beyond what I read in the press and the order of the first administration of the General Staff on the preparation of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that in June 1991 Slovenia and Croatia passed decisions on their secession from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read that in the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Following these decisions by Slovenia and Croatia in late June 1991 concerning the secession -- their secession from Yugoslavia, do you recall the JNA's intervention in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember -- what did you say, "Varazdin court"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall what the task of the JNA units was? They mentioned borders.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, their role was to occupy the key border posts together with the federal police force headed by Commander --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because at the time the federal police force did not hold any ranks as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Prior to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We heard the interpreter say she didn't hear the name of the commander who headed that federal police force. Do you think you can establish the name for us, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Mirko Jokic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was commander of the federal police brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before this intervention, were the -- or did the Slovenian authorities willfully take jurisdiction of the border post along their borders?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the information that I have, too, but it is quite logical that if somebody goes to attack someone else, it means that the other side must have done something unlawful. And the Slovenians had unlawfully taken control of their border. In Yugoslavia it was decided that the border control and border traffic lay within the competence of the federal police and local police, whereas the rest of the border was within the competence of the JNA. So the federal brigade and the local police, since they showed their solidarity -- or rather, it was the local police who showed solidarity with the Slovenian TO, which is why the federal police brigade had to intervene to occupy the border posts, and the JNA forces arrived only at a later stage. This isn't something that I experienced. I read about it. I talked to people who participated in these operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksic. Could you please make sure that in answering your -- my questions, you clearly draw the line between what you experienced personally and what you know from secondary sources. Very often the figure of 1.900 men is used as a force that was sent from Belgrade as the JNA force to intervene in Slovenia. Are you aware of these numbers?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about how many soldiers were sent over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether any armed conflicts ensued in Slovenia, whether the members of the TO and the police force attacked the JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Belgrade archives indicate that the Territorial Defence units attacked the JNA. As far as I remember, 19 soldiers were killed and they were unarmed at that. They had surrendered. However, I did not bother to double-check this particular figure. I'm telling you what I learned from the archives. I also found out something about it from the press; I'm not sure whether it's true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, what does this mean, the fact that 19 unarmed soldiers who had surrendered were killed?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I watched a documentary which showed a soldier holding his position. Two Slovenian armed soldiers appeared. This person threw his weapon down, raised his arms, and the Slovene men shot him. That's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Yugoslav Presidency passed a decision to the effect that the JNA forces provisionally withdraw from Slovenia in order to avoid further casualties, both among the soldiers and the civilians?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the period when the JNA barracks in Croatia were blocked and attacked, if you know the date?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the date. I only know that the blockades of the barracks were mounted, and this is something that is contained in the reports of the JNA units. I know, for instance, about the Varazdin barracks where there was General Trifunovic that was blocked. But others were blocked by the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, what constituted the armed forces of Yugoslavia, which elements were there?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The armed forces of Yugoslavia were made by the JNA, the Territorial Defence, and the civilian protection. However, the Territorial Defence was found to be quite problematic by the military personnel because there were two types of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But we will get back -- get back to that a bit later. I'm interested in something else at the moment. You said that the JNA units and barracks were blocked by the Yugoslav army, but what sort of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: By the Croatian army, Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What sort of a Croatian army are you speaking of in 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who ordered Croatian Territorial Defence to block the barracks?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider such a Territorial Defence of Croatia to be regular military forces, pursuant to the constitution of Yugoslavia, especially in view of them attacking the regular federal armed force, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question contains two questions. The first question I would answer in the following way. The TO of Croatia or of any other republic while the SFRY was still unified represented a regular force, legally established, regular force. As for your second question, I apologise, but I didn't catch it. Did have a right to attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and how do you qualify that?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they had no right to do that, and it can be qualified as a rebellion of part of the units which constitute unified armed forces. It could be termed as armed rebellion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, this took place of Croatia adopted a decision to secede from Yugoslavia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. However, I don't know -- rather, I can't remember the date. The decision on secession is one thing, but whether it was recognised by the international community or other states, that's a different thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Maksic, those are two different issues and we'll get back to that later. Did you hear of an affair involving an airplane known as Kikas affair from Uganda in August of 1991? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to Bajic. This plane landed at the Zagreb airport, if we are having the same affair in mind. The plane was loaded with weapons, and units of the corps led by General Bajic seized the plane and confiscated the weapons. I heard of this from people who partially took part in this operation, if that was your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I had in mind, Mr. Maksic. Do you know any details surrounding the blockades and attacks on the barracks? How was that carried out? Were only individual barracks involved or all of them? Do you know anything about power cuts, water supply cuts, and so on?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are two terms, attacks and blocking the barracks, at least in the military terminology. An attack on barracks is performed with an aim to seize the barracks, the equipment, weaponry, and to use it for own purposes. If that is impossible, then a blockade of barracks is carried out, and all services to the barracks are cut off, all vital supplies necessary for the people in the barracks to survive. This is what a blockade is, because a force that is able to attack will not block. The blockade of the barracks resembles, to a certain extent, the blockade of Troy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this is time for our regular break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we will take a short break and come back at quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, we spoke about the blockades and attacks on the JNA units and garrisons in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. Allow me once again to remind you of the need to make pauses between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, we mentioned the units and barracks of the JNA in the territory of the former Yugoslav Republic of Croatia. These units and barracks that you are aware of, did they exist for many years prior to that in the territory of that republic as well as in the territories of other republics?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that many barracks and garrisons are located in populated areas, in towns and cities, that they were located within an urban centre?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barracks were constructed many years ago, and cities expanded in the meantime and then the barracks found themselves in an urban centre. So your statement is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what was the position of Croatian authorities on the eve of Croatian declaration of independence and after that? What was their position vis-a-vis JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As early as in the beginning of June and July, a large number of officers of Croatian nationality asked for their service in the JNA to be terminated. Many soldiers deserted from the JNA; they flew -- they fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that the information provided by many cabinet members of the government of Franjo Tudjman is true, namely, that the JNA was defeated from within once 17.000 JNA officers and soldiers left and went from the JNA to the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number of officers and soldiers who left the JNA; I know it's a large number. I don't know whether this was done under the influence of the Croatian government or somebody else's influence. I suppose that the recommendation of the Croatian government was such that officers and soldiers of Croatian nationality ought to leave the JNA, not only those who were stationed in Serbia, but also those who were stationed in Macedonia, Bosnia, and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Upon completing military academy in the JNA, does every officer, upon taking a post with the JNA, have to take an oath?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon arrival at the military academy, some 15 days after that, every student has to take an oath which is basically a solemn declaration whereby he promises that he will faithfully serve and protect integrity and sovereignty of every part of Yugoslavia. At the end there was a stipulation stating that in defence of sovereignty and territorial integrity and inviolability of the territory such an officer would be prepared to die. Also at the end of the academy, each officer had to sign an affidavit stating that he would accept the assignment given to him by the personnel administration, wherever that assignment might take him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the JNA officers who were of Croatian nationality upon leaving the JNA would go and join the Croatian formations which were fighting against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know a dozen such cases, and all of them in 1991, upon leaving the JNA or requesting to go into early retirement, went and joined Croatian armed forces, Bacic, Ivan, Basic, Miro, and all of my pals from the army did that. I later read about them, saw them on television, and realised that they were members of Croatian armed forces and they were appointed to very high posts, starting from the commander of a brigade and up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These officers who -- or rather, did these officers, in your view, betray their state, Yugoslavia? Did they join the other side in order to fight Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they betrayed Yugoslavia or not, I think they did and they also violated the constitutions -- constitution and the laws of Yugoslavia. And they would have been prosecuted criminally, had they remained in the territory of Serbia. They violated the constitution and committed a treason in relation to the oath or the solemn declaration that they took and signed, making a promise to the state of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the attacks in the territory of the former Yugoslav Republic of Croatia, the attacks against the JNA units and garrisons represented an armed rebellion. Did the federal state have a constitutional obligation to put down that rebellion?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did, both pursuant to the Law on People's Defence and the Army of Yugoslavia and in accordance with the rules of service. Rules of service represent an excerpt from the law on people's defence. It was something that was available to each officer and soldier in order not to make them read all the laws. This was given to them, presented to them, in the form of an excerpt, which were these rules of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the leadership of Croatia which was in charge of Croatian secession from Yugoslavia called the Yugoslav army the "occupation army" and the "aggressor's army"?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read that in the papers. I read that in official interviews given by the leaders of Croatian state -- or rather Croatian republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, you completed all military schools, including the highest ones. In your view, was the JNA an aggressor's army and the occupation army in its on territory?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. An army cannot be an aggressor's army in its own territory. Therefore, the JNA could under no circumstances, pursuant to any law, be it domestic or an international one, be considered an aggressor's army in its own territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, did you read in the papers or did you hear on television that even in the European community at the time condemned the JNA as the aggressor's army? Is it true?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that they did it; however, that was not a logical step.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "was true"? You mean that it was true that they condemned the JNA but that that wasn't logical?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I meant, they condemned the JNA, not all European countries, certain ones. It wasn't logical for them to condemn the JNA. Most likely they were not familiar with the internal laws regulating the relations between the federal armed forces and the federal state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Yugoslav armed forces have both the right and the duty to operate throughout the territory of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the armed forces of Yugoslavia in their operations in 1991, 1992, through to 1995 ever step beyond the borders, internationally recognised borders, of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, at that point in time did they go beyond the internationally recognised borders of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the event which transpired in Split in May 1991 which was popularly known as the strangling of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know of this event from the TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what happened.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this was a group of Ustasha that rebelled, and there was a group of soldiers which was part of the Split garrison who were normally in charge of maintaining law and order in the area who came out of the barracks in an APC. And one of the men from the group of rebels climbed on top of the APC, drew the -- one of the crew out of the APC and started strangling him. The man who was being strangled was a Macedonian. However, other people jumped to his assistance. The JNA committed a mistake in omitting to bring the perpetrators to justice and prosecuting them. I believe that this was a result of a political agreement between Slovenia and Croatia to calm the situation down and to prevent matters from deteriorating. However, this was a sign of things having gone wrong in the country. The chief of the General Staff and the Federal Secretary for National Defence were duty-bound under the constitution to prevent such acts from happening through the use of their forces, but they failed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in early 1991, in April, the trial started against General Spegelj and some of his associates for illegal distribution of weapons, and do you know what the outcome of this trial in Zagreb was?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that General Spegelj was charged with high treason for importing weapons with a view to using them against the Serb civilians. But however, I know that General Spegelj fled, absconded, to Austria, and that was the end of it. I read about it in the press.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that the blockade of the garrisons and barracks in Croatia were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the witness [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Her Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Put your question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr. Milovancevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Earlier on the witness was being asked to repeat the last sentence before you went into your last question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, for the sake of the record, you were talking about the start of trial against Mr. Spegelj. Can you tell us again what happened and whether the trial was brought to the end.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An indictment was issued against Spegelj, and the trial started; however, several days later Spegelj absconded and fled to Austria as far as I know. I don't know what happened to him later on, but I know that he left the Republic of Croatia before his trial was brought to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of the National Guards Corps, and if you have, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The National Guards Corps is a paramilitary unit which was getting prepared for combat and gathering equipment. Later on it evolved into the Croatian army. The Republic of Croatia illegally imported weapons to equip these units. As far as I know, the National Guards Corps was -- consist -- was made up of volunteers. It was supposed to be the elite unit of the Croatian army in charge of accomplishing all the missions that the other units were unable to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the National Guards Corps units took part in the attacks on the JNA barracks in what was Croatia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether these ZNG units indeed took part in the attacks on the JNA barracks, but I do know that they were the leaders of these attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you clarify this a bit. You are not certain of their participation, but what is your basis -- what is the basis of your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether units themselves, such as a battalion or a company of the ZNG, actually took part in these operations. But I do know that ZNG members, officers were at the head of those who launched these attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I wish to ask you about some events that were quite prominent in the media. Do you know anything about the sufferings of the members of the TO in September 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that a group of men set out to get some supplies and that they were killed over the -- on the Korana bridge. I don't know any other details surrounding this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know you how the Serbian authorities -- or rather, how the Croatian authorities, led by Tudjman, treated the Serbian population in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing I can tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything of the operations of the Croatian forces in Slavonia, Bila Gora, Pakrac, Daruvar?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know only what I read in the press, but that is too little for me to be able to give you any view on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksic. In your earlier testimony you told us that on the 1st of October, 1991, you were sent by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence to the territory of Krajina, namely, Knin. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Which JNA corps was in charge of Knin and of Dalmatia in general?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th Corps of the JNA of the 5th Army. The commander was Tomo Vukovic, who got killed in 1992 or 1993, and the Chief of Staff was Ratko Mladic. I had many dealings with them. I cooperated with them, exchanged information on the situation in the area. He was far better informed than I was. As for the other high-ranking officers there, they rotated quite frequently. The corps command is the commander, Chief of Staff, chief for security, chief for training and operations, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, for the record you stated the name of Mr. Vukovic. Is his name Vladimir or --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vladimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said "Tomo."

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, is it Vladimir Vukovic, General Vladimir Vukovic, commander of the 9th Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I made a mistake because we called him "Tomo," so I used his nickname, rather than his actual first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksic. At the time you arrived in Knin, did the 9th Corps carry out an operation of lifting the blockades of the JNA barracks that were within his -- its area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I heard, Zemunik, the blockade of Zemunik and Sibenik was supposed to be lifted. The same was also true for Sinj, where the assets that were found there were supposed to be taken into the Krajina territory. There was an engineers' regiment in Sinj which held great quantities of equipment. As for Sibenik, Zemunik, Zadar, there were large numbers of troops and amounts of hardware, which had to be pulled out of there. Some of it was pulled out, some of it was left behind. I believe it was on the 30th of September that there was an attempt to pull the equipment out, but the operation was aborted on the order of the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the blockades in Sibenik, Zemunik, and Sinj were supposed to be lifted. What were these features? Were they JNA facilities?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were JNA barracks and JNA features which had to be taken out of the blockade, and I mean troops and equipment, and taken to the Krajina area. It was highly likely that the 9th Corps together with the other forces of Krajina would, in fact, seize Northern Dalmatia, Sinj, and Zemunik. That was the actual balance of power; however, the chief of the General Staff did not give the green light for the action because it was thought that some space should be left for a political solution to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksic. Let us make things quite clear. You said that the 9th Corps was trying to lift the blockade of the JNA features containing equipment and troops. Who was maintaining the blockade of all these JNA buildings?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were these forces the same ones that you mentioned as having committed a rebellion?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those same ones. We - and when I say -- I mean, we're talking about matters that are in the realm of operations and tactics. When a rebellion emerges in a country, it is usually resolved and crushed with own forces. There would have been no difficulty for the JNA, with the forces that it had in its possession, including the air force, all of which were under the command of General Bajic, to resolve this matter entirely. However, it was left to the political sphere to resolve the matter so that the army ever since 1991 was the victim of politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the JNA had enough troops and equipment and weapons - and I mean the 9th Corps - to seize Sibenik, Zemunik, Sinj. Did it have enough forces to capture and seize Split as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because once you seize Zadar, Split automatically falls.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, you said that the JNA refrained from this action because of the decision to resolve it politically?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that it refrained; it was banned from doing that. Ultimately it was the Presidency that disallowed it and opted for the political solution; therefore, it was a stop-go/stop-go situation all the while, and the JNA did not have a clear situation in which it could orient itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about 1991. Who was at the head of the Presidency of the SFRY at the time? Wasn't it Stjepan Mesic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. Don't take me on that one, but I believe, yes, it was Stipe Mesic who uttered this famous statement of his which became part of history of political science that he -- his mission was accomplished and that Yugoslavia was no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was Ante Markovic prime minister of Yugoslavia? Was the foreign minister Budimir Loncar, both of them Croats?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have trouble with dates and names. I can't be specific when it comes to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksic. Did you know that Zemunik was supposed to be deblocked? What is Zemunik? What was located there?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some units there, air force academy, air force secondary school. There were also some formations of the air force there as well which were quite significant for armed combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was there an airport there as well used by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course there was an airport. It was an air force base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So the task of the 9th Corps of the JNA was to deblock all of these cities, Sibenik, Zadar, and so on, plus Zemunik.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As you know, it is not proper to speak ill of the death, of the dead people, and I spoke to -- to the commander who was in charge. I also had opportunity to see his decision concerning Sibenik, Zadar, Zemunik, and so on which were supposed to be taken militarily. The attack had already been launched so that people from Sibenik, Zadar, Zemunik were already leaving populated settlements in boats and so on. However, some way -- somewhere half into the operation when the operation was in its greatest swing and when all branches and services of the JNA were involved, we found ourselves at that point in time at the command post. Everything was going fine, I mean for those attacking. And then all of a sudden an order arrived sometime at around 3.00 a.m. to pull everything back to starting positions. The order arrived from the chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did that mean "militarily"? Was it positive for the JNA units or for the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the JNA units which took part in the attack, not only the JNA units but also forces of municipal TO and police which were also engaged, and I don't have information on their numbers, represented a disappointment and harassment. And this dealt a blow to the morale of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see OTP document 1857 from the 65 ter list, please. This was exhibited as Exhibit P49.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before this document comes up on our monitors, Mr. Maksic, I will tell you that this is a document of the 9th Corps command dated the 31st of October, 1991, which is entitled "order for assault operation on Sibenik, operations number 2, excerpt for the Territorial Defence staff of SAO Krajina." Did you see this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is an excerpt from the order of the corps commander for assault operation on Sibenik. See, we don't have a map here, but if Sibenik were to fall, Zadar, and Split would fall as well. This is an excerpt intended for the TO Staff of Krajina for them to be informed of what was planned in the assault operation as well as of the role and place of the TO units. However, I saw the integral order. This is just an excerpt, and that is precisely what is stated here. You can see in the second line. It says: "Excerpt for the TO Staff," which means that this is not an integral order of the 9th Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Based on the text in paragraph 2, 3, 4, and 5 on page 1 where Croatian forces are discussed, based on that text is it clear that these were armed and equipped Croatian forces that the JNA was supposed to engage and implement the mission that it was assigned?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, the information provided in paragraphs 1 through 5, this is what you have in mind. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information was obtained via intelligence activity of the security organ of the 9th Corps. The security organ of the 9th Corps -- am I going it too fast?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, that's quite fine.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organ of the 9th Corps concluded, established, conducted reconnaissance, and so on and came to conclusion that the 113th Brigade of the ZNG was engaged in that area, that there was a police company with a -- one to two detachments of the Territorial Defence. I'm not sure what it says here, or maybe this is the APCs, two mortars and so on. So the intelligence officers of the 9th Corps acquired information as to what was in the territory that they were supposed to be deployed to and take.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, does it state in paragraph 2 that in defence of Sibenik there is the 113th Brigade of the ZNG engaged without one battalion, up to two police battalions of the police administration of Sibenik, about two companies of armed locals, then cannons, four by 130, and cannons, six by 80-80, and up to two artillery pieces of 85-millimetres. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely correct what you read out, counsel. And then where it says on the stretch, Cista Mala Gacelezi Juzno and so on, there is the 2nd Battalion of the 113th Brigade, and everything else you enumerated is correct. I don't know whether it was correct. The intelligence people claimed that this was correct. Based on this information, the planning of these forces was implemented in view of the resources of the 9th Corps, which had an artillery regiment for several divisions and so on. And when you take that into account, you will see that the forces on the other side were quite insufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksic. Let us take a look at page 3, the last four digits of that page are 4463, the ERN digits. Before it comes up on the screen I will read the text to you, and then later on you can confirm whether I read it out correctly.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Great. What was the mission of the 9th Corps? What does General Vukovic say? Can you read it out for us?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the -- yeah, that's good. Yeah, just a little bit more. Scroll down. Yes, that's good, that's fine. Item 4. In -- each order specifies what the commander has decided. It says here: "I have decided to use strong artillery and air force support in coordination with parts of the military naval district, 84th air force base, and the units of Territorial Defence of SAO Krajina to use main forces of the corps to attack Sibenik," which means that the main goal was to attack Sibenik. And I told you why Sibenik was so important, because if Sibenik fell, then Split and Zadar fell as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Would you please read to us the section which is entitled "mission," which is just a little bit above?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you scroll up?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Item 3 -- above item 3 are the words "mission" or "task."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please scroll up on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a little bit more, please, where it says "mission."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please read out "mission" for us.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Crush enemy forces and seize roads. Arrive at the outskirts of Sibenik. Introduce the 2nd Operations Echelon" -- may I clarify this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please read until the end, and then you can explain to us.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Continue action, deblock personnel and all military facilities in Sibenik, repulse the attack or forces from the town, create necessary time for relocation of deblocked technical and combat resources and personnel, encircle and force enemy forces to surrender."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's enough, Mr. Maksic. Do you have any comments? Does this confirm what you told us just prior?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 1st Echelon is to go and pierce the defence line, and these people will suffer great losses. And then this will bring them to the outskirts of Sibenik. This is where they have to stop because they have no power anymore. They have used up their power in order to get there. And then the 2nd Operative Echelon is introduced which is supposed to carry on the mission and do what I read out under this section "mission," namely, to deblock and pull out the resources, whereas those forces, enemy forces remaining in Sibenik are to be encircled and destroyed. I can explain to you what it means to destroy them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, we will get to that later. Will you please now turn to page 7 which has ERN number 4467. Could we see item 7, please, which is entitled "moral support." Could you please scroll up a little bit so we can see item 7.2 in its entirety, please. In item 7.2, Mr. Maksic, would you please read out the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Prior to the beginning of assault operation, informed entire personnel on the goal and necessity of conducting further combat activity no in order to deblock units in the Sibenik garrison. Pull out huge combat resources and full disarmament of enemy forces of MUP and the so-called ZNG," which is the National Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksic. Now the penultimate paragraph in this section "moral support" -- or rather, the last one, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Shall I read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Prevent looting, revenge, torching of houses and other facilities; and in this manner, spread trust in the forces which are conducting combat; inform soldiers of detrimental effects of such incidents, especially reiterate the importance of preserving religious -- especially reiterate the need for preserving religious facilities, cathedrals, churches, and cultural monuments."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What you just read out, Mr. Maksic, is it in other words with the information that you had about the goals and missions of the 9th Corps at the time in September and October -- or rather, while the 9th Corps was active in its area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the indictment the Prosecution claims the opposite, namely, that that wasn't goal, but rather that the goal was to use the JNA, the police, the Territorial Defence, and volunteers which they call Serb forces, and says that it was their goal to encircle the villages, to use aviation, artillery, to force the population to flee, and then to have the besieging forces enter such villages, kill all the remaining population, and set property on fire, and so on. Do you have such information? Did you hear of such a thing, Mr. Maksic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have such a document. I never heard of that. Is there such a document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm putting to you what the Prosecution claims, and I'm asking you whether this is true.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a single written or oral order contains anything of that nature. This was not done either by military or police officers. Why am I saying this? I don't know all police officers, senior officers, and inspectors, but I know a lot of them. I know how they were schooled. I also organised training for police personnel. And not a single Yugoslav soldier was ever told anything this ugly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, you say that you stayed in the territory of Knin and Krajina from the 1st of October until the end of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
