utterances.text: You said that you held meetings with various people, politicians, including the most influential politicians, Martic and Babic, who were the most influential at the time; that you also met with commanders and members of TO staffs, with the JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear from any of them that there was an idea, a plan, an order, a suggestion to kill all non-Serb population, to make them flee, to drive them away in order to attach this territory to a new Serb state?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer your first question. Yes, I held a lot of meetings, not official ones but also official ones, mostly with Milan Babic as supreme commander of the armed forces of Krajina. I never heard from him anything of the sort, although he was quite a narrow-minded person when it comes to the military and Krajina. You know, he would, for example, point out to me, the barracks are here, Krajina would go up to here, but he would never say that there were no Croats in that area, that Croats would be driven out; rather, he spoke about the territory, not the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksic.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met with Martic several times, but I never discussed these matters with him, I never asked him anything to that effect or anything of the sort. But I know what I saw. I saw the police force -- how I saw them behave, and I never saw any members of the police force discriminate against people along the ethnic lines, that they ever made the distinction that this person was a Serb and the other a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt, please, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Maksic told us that he held a lot of meetings, not official ones but also official ones, mostly with Milan Babic. And then he goes on for quite some time up to the end of that paragraph. Then you say: "Thank you, Mr. Maksic." And then he says: "I met with Martic several times." Are we talking about Martic or are we talking about Babic? I'm just not quite sure what's happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: For clarity's sake, you said you had several meetings with Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And that you met with Martic only rarely and for brief periods?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss these matters with Mr. Martic and did he ever say that anybody had to be killed or chased away because the person was of a different ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never discussed these matters with him. It would have been out of place for me to discuss these matters with him, but I talked to other members of the police force and we discussed these matters. Martic's police never made any distinction between the perpetrators of a crime along their ethnic line, whether a perpetrator was a Serb or a Croat. They were treated in the same way, and that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksic. In your statement for the OTP, and I believe also during your testimony here, you said that you were shown documents governing the action on Saborsko, which is a small village near the Plitvice lake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show Prosecution Exhibit 1251 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do -- before we do that, what must we do with this one that's on the screen right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that document is already a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's already in the file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document 1251. This is the 65 ter number, and this is already an exhibit, 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before this document comes up on the screen, I will tell you, Mr. Maksic, that according to the heading of the document this is the order for attack, operations number 2, addressed to the command of the Tactical Group 2. I believe we have it on our screens now. Mr. Maksic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the document on the screen and do you see that it is indeed the command of the 13th Corps and that the document is dated 7th November 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will refer you to item 1 of the order which reads: "The forces of the MUP and the ZNG Croatia have been making fortifications for some time now in the area of the villages of Borik, Saborsko, Funtana, Panjici, and Kuselj. It is estimated that the strength of the forces in the area is of some 400 members of the paramilitary formations. There is information indicating that some of these extremist Ustasha are ready, dug-in and prepared for a long-lasting struggle." Let's move down and look at the point where it says: "So far the following firing positions were observed in the area of the village of Borik, north-south there are six machine-gun emplacements, and at the other end of the village, the southern end of the village, some 50 Ustasha are to be found in houses." Then it says: "South of the village Tuk there is a machine-gun emplacement and south of the village of Brdine there are two sub-machine-gun emplacements. To the north-west of the trigonometric point Alan there are 738 82-millimetre mortars, or rather, there are seven -- that trigonometric point 748 there is an unknown number of 82-millimetre mortars and in a grove there is a group of houses where there was a group of 200 Ustasha, and they were attacked by aviation. In the village of Saborsko, estimates are that there are 150 Ustasha and as many in the village of Funtana as well. In Mali Sivnik there is an unknown number of 82-millimetre mortars, and west of two dirt roads there is a machine-gun and a sub-machine-gun emplacement. In the region of Razvala there is also a sub-machine-gun emplacement. In the village of Kuselj -- in addition to the losses that they have we noticed enemy forces of an unknown strength. As far as we can tell, the enemy is well-prepared in organising of ambushes, and the firing system is -- has been put in place and is able to attack all the approach roads to the settled places and open areas and protect its own forces in the pull-out." Therefore, this is an order of the command of the 13th Corps to the Tactical Group 2. Can we conclude on the basis of this that this was an organised taking-up of positions and firing points and that the enemy has put in place an entire defence system, that's to say the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen this document for the first time yesterday, and I tried to make out something of it but I haven't been able to. This being on the 11th -- the 7th of November, I wouldn't know about anything being planned along those lines. I know that nothing of the sort was, in fact, implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see this particular document? This is an order dated 7th November.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen this document. This is an order signed by Cedo Bulat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Maksic, can we take a look at the page to see who signed the order. This is page 7777, page 5 of this order for attack. Who signed the document?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This was sent by the command of the 13th Corps, and this was a forward command post in the village of Mukinje and it was issued on the 7th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this. I was in the area for some four or five days in 1991 -- in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, I'm interested in the following. The order for attack issued by whatever commander, in this case it's the 13th Corps, shouldn't such an order state the strength of the enemy forces that the own forces are to face?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, they would state the intelligence that they obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does the document before you contain such figures? Aren't the contents of this document in fact quite logical?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the data contained in paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if they're true. This commander, Slobodan Djordjevic - I have to tell you as an aside that I never heard of him - signed the document, but it doesn't bear a stamp, which means that the order itself is non-binding and null and void. Can we look at the next page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please show the second page, page 2 of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, when an order is drafted it is signed. It also states who, in fact drafted it, who signed it. There's a stamp, and then it also says who it was delivered to. Can we turn to the next page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back to the beginning of the document? This is page 3. Could we go back to page 773.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this particular case against Mr. Martic, this fact should not be in dispute; it should be substantiated by a series of documents and witness statements. It's a fact that on the 12th of November, the Tactical Group 2 under the command of Colonel Cedo Bulat conducted the operation called the attack on Saborsko. What I'm showing to you now is a document in the possession of the OTP which was obtained from an archive; I don't know if it's an original or not. I merely wanted you to confirm that the contents of the document are consistent with what is normally written in an order.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But normally a document bears a stamp; in that way it is certified. The document, as it is now, is not certified and I could have well written it myself. When the stamp is affixed to the document, this guarantees that the person who signed the document in fact wrote the document. I wish to tell you as an aside that I was trying yesterday to locate these villages on the map, Saborsko, Funtana, Panjici, but I haven't been able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document as a whole is not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then we won't be dealing with it anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask that we be shown the last page of the original document, in other words, the B/C/S document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please show page 7777 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you scroll down, please. Okay. Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, you spoke of the action that was carried out by the 9th Corps to lift the blockade?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The action aimed at deblocking these features, what was its outcome, do you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you really how this was implemented. I know that elements of the forces were pulled out; I don't know in what way. I only talked of the operation carried out on the 31st of October, I believe - that's the date of the order - when this was in fact to be done. We were at the command post in Drnis. There was Vukovic, Djujic, and I was there. I'm not sure, but I believe that Mr. Martic was there as well. And from there, we followed the course of the deblocking operation when, in fact, the action was aborted and the forces pulled back to their starting positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is my understanding right that you speak of the time when the attacks were launched and the Croats were already getting on boats to flee the area?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The SAO Krajina units with the 9th Corps, which was in fact in charge of the entire operation, were advancing and they were getting close to Zadar. The Croatian forces started leaving the area, boarding boats, to flee by sea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to have to interrupt. There's one time when two of you were talking and the interpreter was talking. I'm not quite sure how the poor interpreter copes. Could we please go slow. I see it's also 12.00, Mr. Milovancevic. How much longer do you want to go on before we break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think this is a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We'll adjourn and we'll come back at half past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, can we remember to please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, on the 1st of October you went to Krajina in Knin, where you remained until the end of December 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could it be said that in that period of time in the area of responsibility of the 9th Corps of the JNA, which is where Knin was, there existed a state of armed conflict or there existed armed operations?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that there were problems with mobilisation. You said that Croats had left. The 9th Corps of the JNA was not a Serb force, but there was a significant problem with mobilisation. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was it only the conscripts of Croat nationality who left the JNA in 1991, or did members of other nationalities do the same? And if so, which ones? Do you know anything about that? In order for you to understand --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order for you to understand my question, I'm referring to conscripts from Slovenia, Macedonia, and Bosnia, including Serbia.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left it, too, not in mass numbers, but there were individual cases of desertion. People went back to Macedonia, to Bosnia, to Serbia. I'm now referring to active soldiers, not reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that upon your arrival in Knin, you saw that whoever was fit for military service had been mobilised either into the JNA or the Krajina police?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, plus the municipal TO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you explained that in order to create the Krajina TO Staff, you needed 25 to 30 people and that only four of you were sent to complete that mission, yourself, Colonel Djujic, and another two officers?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the order of the head of personnel department of the 20th of September, 24 or 25 people were supposed to be sent, however, only four went, the four that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that the order of the Federal Secretariat for People's Defence, the order of commands subordinated to it envisioned that 24, 25 officers were supposed to be sent to Knin to perform that task, and that only four of you responded to the order?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that starting from the 1st of October until the end of December, throughout your stay in Knin and Krajina, you did not receive a single instruction, a single order from the Ministry of Defence of Serbia pertaining to the organisation of Territorial Defence in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order to avoid any confusion in the transcript, you are confirming that you did not receive any such order?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received no orders, no information. We also did not receive any instructions on the formation of the TO Staff of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, you explained that from August 1991 Krajina TO sent a number of documents to the Ministry of Defence of Serbia and the General Staff requesting equipment and weapons. Were these requests ever responded to?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said something similar, but I phrased it differently. I said that I found documents signed by the Minister of Defence -- or rather, the Secretary of Defence, I am not quite sure. I found requests by Mr. Martic for certain equipment that was needed to equip the staff and also TO staff units. This request was not sent to the General Staff, but rather the Ministry of Defence of Serbia. In October this request was expanded and supplemented and sent again by us. We received no reply and no equipment except for several telephones, field telephones that were very old. We received 30 to 40 of them, and they were not operational. With our units and with our staffs in the entire territory of Krajina, we could not communicate. We used police communication lines. Sometimes we used the postal service, fax, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see on the monitor OTP document 211 from the 65 ter list. This is Exhibit 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is a request for ammunition and other type of military equipment sent to the Ministry of Defence of Serbia in Belgrade personally to the minister, Mr. Simovic. The request was sent from Knin on the 18th of September, 1991. Mr. Maksic, we saw this request on our monitors. It has several pages, and it contains a list of the equipment needed for the Territorial Defence of Knin, Benkovac TO, Obrovac TO, and municipalities.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all municipalities, Gracac, Vrgin Most, Vojnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is a list containing all the rifles, combat sets, and other types of equipment needed. Is this the document that you had in mind when you said that you saw a request which was not responded to?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, another issue is important here. I'm reading now. "In relation to your telegram, strictly confidential 5-259 dated 12th of September, 1991, we are sending you the list of the supplies needed by SAO Krajina." Based on this request, we can conclude that the Ministry of Defence of Serbia sent a telegram either to the minister or the secretary of defence of Krajina, asking that a list of supplies needed be sent to them. This list sent -- or rather, the Ministry of Defence of Serbia sent a telegram to the Secretary of Defence of Krajina, asking that he send them a list of needed supplies. Based on the telegram, we can conclude Mr. Martic collected information from the municipal TO staffs and then compiled them and sent the list of equipment and weapons needed by the municipal TO staffs. This is what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksic. You said that in addition to this request there were also other requests, renewed requests, but that you received nothing in return, except for those 30 to 40 telephones?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please scroll up?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, we need the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Further, please. Further, please, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We need the second page.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or perhaps the last page. It doesn't matter. Can we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you move down the document, please, for Mr. Maksic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see further, the end of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please show us the last portion of the document, page 7601, page 9 of the document. Can we please scroll to the end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. That's fine. I've read it. You see, this was signed by Minister Martic, this request, this request representing the total requests coming from all municipalities. You can see here: "Minister Milan Martic." All right, all right. And there is also a signature by "TO commander." I suppose that they merged the two. This document was found in the archives of the command of the Knin TO Staff, and we used it as a basis for writing a renewed request to the ministry of Serbia, a renewed and supplemented request. We received no reply saying whether we would receive the approximate supplies requested or not. What came in the form of a reply were those telephones that I told you, and we either sent them back or gave them to Colonel Jakovljevic to take them back because they were unusable, could not be repaired. Even if we had repaired them, we could not use them for our communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, in order to clarify what kind of telephones these are, you said these were induction telephones. What kind of system is this?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was something introduced 30 or 40 years prior to that in the JNA units. It was produced by a factory in Nis. They were battery operated, and their range was intended either for companies or platoons. They were outdated. They were stored in depots for years and were supposed to be decommissioned. I had many of them in my facility. We didn't know what to do with them. We thought maybe we should send them back to the factory to see if they could use them in what way. We were not allowed to throw them away; we had to store them and keep them for years. It should be clearly stated that this was an act of destruction on the part of the Ministry of Defence of Serbia, vis-a-vis the Republic of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksic. Let me ask you something else. You drew a chart of the Krajina TO, and on the top you put "Ministry of Defence of Serbia," explaining that this vertical line showed how the Krajina TO was dependent in every sense, technical, personnel, professional sense, dependent on the Ministry of Defence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your replies you explained that upon your arrival in Knin you found a situation in which everybody who was fit for military service had been mobilised either into the JNA units or the police units --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- or municipal TO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us make sure that we do not overlap for the sake of interpreters. Can you tell us whether the Krajina police in the operations of the 9th Corps was resubordinated to that corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Krajina police perform some tasks that were assigned by the 9th Corps command?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depended on the Minister of the Interior and the 9th Corps commander. It depended on how they coordinated and jointly performed their tasks. If the 9th Corps commander needed elements of the forces of the police, he was duty-bound to get in touch with the Minister of the Interior and ask whether the minister would provide his forces or not. If yes, then they had to coordinate the way this was to be implemented. However, the -- the 9th Corps commander could not order the minister to provide him with, say, 100 men for some operation; they had to coordinate resubordination. It was a matter of their cooperation and coordinated action. They met every Monday for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That sort of cooperation, was it in accordance with the SFRY constitution and the law on the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Ministry of the Interior of SAO Krajina, regardless of who the minister was, whenever the 9th Corps had to carry out some operations and sought coordination and cooperation, did it -- the ministry have the obligation to get in touch and see to it that the assistance is provided?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was duty-bound to see whether it can assist the army; however, this was within the scope of their abilities. If the minister was of the opinion that this exceeded their capacities, then they were not able to assist. I believe that this is what the regulations say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, we heard of the deblocking action carried out by the 9th Corps in September, October, and later on in 1991. Do you know whether the other JNA units whose area of responsibility covered parts of Croatia had any duties in that operation?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what operation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the operation of deblocking the JNA facilities and pulling people out.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean in the same area of responsibility as that of the 9th Corps or in other parts of the Republic of Croatia like in Varazdin?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, my question to you was the following: Regardless of the unit involved, were operations of this sort carried out in other parts of what is today the Republic of Croatia by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was the Federal Secretary for National Defence or other Chief of General Staff's directives to make sure that the JNA equipment and troops are deblocked. To this end, I took part in an operational action which was partly coordinated by the air force commanded over by Bajic, but I don't know of any others and what they did. I cannot tell you. I don't have any reliable information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksic. There is information to the effect that the JNA until the UN decided to deploy the blue helmets in Croatia in January, February 1992, that in this period the JNA had concluded 14 truces. Do you agree with that? Is that consistent with the information you have that?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the territory of Yugoslavia, do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of 12 truces. It is possible that there were 14, but I am sure of these 12, although probably the information you gave is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who issued the order for such truces? Was it done by the JNA alone or --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was done by the political leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the political leadership of Yugoslavia in fact the SFRY Presidency? Was the Presidency the commander-in-chief of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, they were not able to reach an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, are you familiar with the statement of the president of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Franjo Tudjman, that he gave in May 1992, a year after the declaration of Croatia's independence when in the central square of Banjelici [phoen] in Zagreb in front of TV cameras he stated: "There would have been no war had Croatia not desired it. It was the only way for us to achieve independence"?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence has finished its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Ms. Richterova, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, a very short one. I only want to find exact quotes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, the Defence counsel asked you or put to you whether you know anything about the fact that the goals of the JNA, police, TO, and other forces would be to kill, to expel people from the territory, et cetera. And your answer was: No, not a single written or oral order which would contain anything like this, ordering any kind of crime. And you also stated: "I saw the police force, how they behave, and I never saw any members of the police force discriminating against people along the ethnic lines, that they ever made the distinction that these people would be -- that this person was a Serb and the other a Croat." Here you are referring to police forces. Would it be the same to say about JNA soldiers or members of the TO?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the first part but not the last.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: My question was whether what you said about the police forces, is that they never made any distinction along the ethnic lines, whether the same refers to the JNA or TO members.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness document 65 ter 2060. This document is dated 4th of October, 1991, and it is from Territorial Defence Staff Glina municipal. Can you scroll down a little bit. Thank you. Like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you please read this order?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To all units of the TO Glina. "When mopping up the terrain, spare Pajo Bubas and his wife, who is a Serb, and their home. They have been verified as loyal people. The house is in Toplicka street, Aleksa Santeka 3. "Anyone who does not abide by this order will be severely punished. This order shall come into force immediately. "TO commander, Captain First Class, Stanko Divjakinja."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Based on what you said before, what would be the purpose -- or why would this document be necessary, this order be necessary?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an isolated case which was not typical of the relations in Republika Srpska. This is just something that this particular person states, but I don't know what the context is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksic, you answered my question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it not already?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, this hasn't been tendered yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit Number 133, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, a few questions from the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I will -- I must apologise at the beginning. I know absolutely nothing about military issues and the army, so I'm going to ask you very basic questions for my own understanding. Apart from a soldier, what is the next smallest unit in an army?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The smallest unit is a squad, which numbers up to ten people, up to ten men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Above the squad --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eight to ten men. A platoon. A platoon has four squads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Above a platoon?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Above a platoon is a company, which has four platoons. We're talking of infantry units here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm still going to ask you what an infantry is. Above a company?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many companies is a battalion made of, if it is made of companies?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's got four -- four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Four? It's got four what? Four companies? And then above a battalion?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Made up of?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three battalions, an artillery battalion, headquarters, signals platoon. Those are the main units of a regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh. You said three battalions, artillery battalion. What else? Headquarters.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A signals platoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, what is an artillery battalion, which forms part of the regiment?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Artillery battalion, "divizjon" [phoen] as it is called, are artillery units, cannons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I get -- can I understand you clearly, Mr. Maksic. When we started I was asking you about the people who compose each one of these divisions in a -- in an army. You started off by saying: A squad has ten men. A platoon has four squads, which means it should be 40 men. A company has four platoons. Now -- and I understood you to be talking of people. Now, when you talk of artillery battalion and you mention cannons -- did you mention cannons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, he did mention cannons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm getting confused. I'm still talking about people. You can tell me how all these divisions are armed, but at the moment I just want to know the number of people that compose these various divisions. Are we together?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 150.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 150 what?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Make what, an artillery battalion? Or what do they make?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, headquarters, how many men?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Headquarters or staff command, about 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And single platoon -- single platoon -- is it singles or signals?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Signals platoon, about 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What comes above a regiment?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And how -- of what is a brigade composed in terms of manpower.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A brigade is of a mixed composition. Its numbers may differ, but about 7.000 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And above a brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Made up of?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Its composition is also mixed. It can have infantry regiments, artillery regiments, engineers regiments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: More or less how many men?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may number roughly 7.000 to 9.000 men, depending on its structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And above a division?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And how big would a corps be?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 10 to 15.000 men, again it depends on the structure which is mixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we have been hearing about the 9th Corps. As the army we see in this area, was the entire Army of the SAO Krajina composed of only that one corps, the 9th Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA, yes. Those were the JNA forces, which consisted of the 9th Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What had become of the other corps, the 1st to the 8th Corps and any beyond 9, if there were any?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps were not numbered from lowest to highest number, from 1 to 8. There were the 13th, 15th, 17th beside the 9th, and they covered as their area of responsibility the entire Yugoslavia. One corps was -- or rather, two -- or let's say one was in Bosnia, in Tuzla. One was in Kragujevac. One was in Belgrade. One was in Nis. There was one corps in Kumanova. There was a corps in Sarajevo, another one in Mostar, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the area of responsibility or the area of operation of the 9th Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of the 9th Corps covered Northern Dalmatia and Lika.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In which province is -- are Northern Dalmatia and Lika?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't understand the question. What do you mean "province"? You mean in which republic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In which republic indeed, sorry.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Would I be right then to say the 9th Corps was operating in the Republic of Croatia? Was it covering the entire Republic of Croatia or was it only covering Lika and the other area and Northern Dalmatia?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only Lika and Northern Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Maksic. Now --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I'm not done with you.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm here at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us of special-purpose police which were operating in Knin. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was their special purpose in Knin? What did they do?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not talk of the special unit in Knin which had a special purpose; rather, I talked of the special-purpose unit which was part of the Ministry of the Interior. The Ministry of the Interior had one special-purpose unit which was duty-bound to intervene in crisis areas, to destroy infiltrated sabotage groups, to prevent minor rebellions, and such-like. Regular police units were not equipped enough or mobile enough for that sort of task. The 9th Corps had a similar type of unit, which was the military police battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the 9th Corps operated in Dalmatia and Lika, Northern Dalmatia and Lika?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I've got a longish quotation to quote for you here, I hope you can remember it, from your evidence yesterday. You said: "In 1991 the mobilisation system which was known until then ceased to exist in the territory of Krajina. The 9th Corps was not a Serbian corps within the 9th Corps. There were Croats serving there," and you mentioned a number of points. What I do want to ask you -- I don't want to repeat the whole quotation -- you indicated that: "Once these units were disbanded in order to reinforce the JNA units, some people wanted to join police units and some wanted to join the JNA units." You remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You remember that. Could you clarify whether these TO unit -- TO soldiers were given an operation to go into the MUPs, police? In other words, what I'm trying to find out when you say: "Some wanted to join the JNA units and others wanted to join the police units," did they have an option? Did they have a choice, or were they forced to -- wherever they wanted to join?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war army is composed of reservists. That's what our system is. The 9th Corps had 20 to 30 per cent of such soldiers. This was a mixed ethnic composition. 20 to 30 per cent of soldiers who were Croats left the corps, and the corps had to be reinforced to compensate for those who had left. The people who were used to reinforce the corps came from the TO units. The next priority was the Ministry of the Interior; however, they needed fewer people. Once the corps was filled up and the Ministry of the Interior units, then whoever was left went to serve in the TO units within municipal TO staffs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So this was by way of conscription? There was no choice?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All defence offices within municipalities had records. Everybody was listed in the records. Based on the records, they were sent -- and based on the assignment within their records, they went to the units to which they had been assigned. They were mobilised. They were unable to choose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You also testified that -- yesterday that in the TO staff there were only four of you, and I think even this morning just a few minutes ago when you were being cross-examined you said the same thing. And you indicated that there were -- there were just no units in your group. My question to you is: Where were all these soldiers that were supposed to be forming part of the group or part of the army?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were within the JNA units, the Ministry of the Interior, and the TO units, but those which belonged to municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who was in control of those units that were in the TO of the municipalities and -- who were not with you?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were under the control of municipal presidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And to whom were the municipal presidents answerable at -- at republic level?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the president of the Republic of Krajina, Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And your group where you were only four, who were you answerable to?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Babic, president of the republic. We were his professional agency for the defence of Krajina. We were military professional agency or organ. The idea was for us to set-up one or two brigades of manoeuvre nature which would be able to act in the territory of Lika, Kordun in coordination with the 9th Corps, Ministry of the Interior, and so on to carry out certain operations as needed. However, since the men were mobilised into the 9th Corps, the Ministry of the Interior or the local TO units, there was nobody else left but men who were above 65 and they were of no use. One could not set-up a unit with them. So we were our own goal and purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm getting a bit lost. From your testimony yesterday I got the impression that you said, and please correct me if I'm wrong, that you and three others were manning one office and you had no units underneath you. And -- and you also indicated that there were lots of units elsewhere, but you didn't give the impression yesterday that these two units were answerable to the same person. You actually indicated yesterday that Babic only had political power, and the one who had soldiers under him had real power. Do you remember saying that? Do you remember that, Mr. Maksic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh. I said: Correct me if I'm wrong, did you say yesterday that -- that Babic only had political power with four of you under him, but that the entire soldiers, whatever they were TO or what, were in another group which was not answerable to Babic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they were under the command of presidents of municipalities, and they, in turn, were under the command of Babic, who was the president of the Republic of Krajina. Therefore, via presidents of municipalities, Babic was able to affect the manner in which the municipal TO units was used. Was I clear or shall I explain again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me try and quote to you what I think you said yesterday. You said: "Those which did not join the 9th Corps became Territorial Defence units, based on the capabilities of a municipality. If municipality was a small one, it had a small unit; if it was a large one, it had a large unit. Some TO units became units of the Ministry of the Interior, and then whatever was left was used to establish Territorial Defence units. And as I said, it depended on the resources in the municipality." Do you remember saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I repeated just now, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior and the TO units, it wasn't a case where the TO units in their entirety went to the Ministry of the Interior, no. That wasn't the case. The number that the Ministry of the Interior needed was mobilised into the Ministry of the Interior, the number of men, not entire units. It's just that certain men were mobilised into the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I'm probably failing to put my questions clearly to you. Let me get on to the next one. This morning you said that the year you attended [indiscernible] where you were attending was the 37th year. That was the time you were being asked about having been in college in 1961 and then in 1985, 20 years later, something happened. And you said: "The year I attended was the 37th." I want to find out what it is that you attended. Can you remember that statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't even born in 1937.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. You were not saying you were born in 1937; you were saying it was the 37th year. Now, I didn't know the 37th of what? That's why I wanted to find out from ...

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I said that I was head of the 34th and 37th year or class, 34 and 37 of the military academy of land forces. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's what I wanted to understand. Again today you talked about Kikas affair. I don't -- I'm pronouncing it how it is spelled. I might be mispronouncing it in the B/C/S. That's when you talked about a plane from Uganda.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you tell me more about that. I didn't understand what you were saying about this Kikas -- what is the Kikas affair?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it was from Uganda or not, but as far as I can remember -- once again, it could have been from another country, but this is what happened. I saw TV footage and I read in the papers, it was also discussed -- or rather, I discussed it with the man who was there. It involved a cargo plane which was full of weapons and military equipment and landed at the airport in Zagreb without any customs declarations, permits, or whatever such documents are called. Then, commander of the 4th or 5th Air Force Corps forced the plane to land, seized the plane, and confiscated the weapons which had been imported illegally by Croatia. They were smuggling weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You also talked this afternoon about men killed on the Korana bridge. You were ...

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I read about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's something you read about. Okay. Do you know who they were killed by?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know who they were killed by?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. What was written about was that people who secured the bridge stopped them to check the contents of what they were transporting. They had some food items, flour, and so on, whatever the supply platoon transported. They took them out and killed them, at least that's the extent of what I read. Whether it's true or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You testified that from the 1st of October, 1991, to the end of December 1991 you were in Knin and Krajina.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Prior to the 1st of October, 1991, where were you?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was head of training and operations centre of the Belgrade Corps, defence of the town, and occasionally I substituted for the Chief of Staff for the defence of Belgrade. Prior to that I was commander of 151st Regiment for four years and commander of 505th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After December 1991, where were you?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back to my post which I held prior to that, head of training and operations department of the defence of Belgrade. Then I was offered another post, a higher one. I rejected the offer, and I retired in 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said yesterday also that Milan Babic had no right to appoint you because you had a prior appointment. Is that the appointment in Belgrade you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The sole authority for appointment rested with the federal secretary for defence, and he transferred these competences to the chief of General Staff. It pertained both to my post and my promotion, therefore there was nobody else who were authorised to effect my service in any way. In addition to that, Babic had no legal basis for doing that. Thirdly, he would have done me a disservice because I would have lost the post that I had held for many years prior to that. I did not come to Krajina to become commander of the Krajina TO; I came there to assist, to see if something could be done. I didn't manage to accomplish almost anything, and this is why I regret going there in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Today under cross-examination you indicated that you tried to look for some areas on the map which had been mentioned to you and you couldn't find them.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are locations that were mentioned in the order shown to me. They pertain to some tactical groups. They may have existed, I don't know. It is possible that somebody produced these documents without having any basic knowledge of how military correspondence is to be drafted; therefore, I don't know anything about the origin of these documents, why they were drafted, and whether things were the way they were depicted in these documents. It is possible that they were, but I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Maksic. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any questions arising from the questions from the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have two short questions just to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You answered to the Judge's questions that TO units were answerable to the president of the municipality and that president of the municipality was answerable further to Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How was it when the TO units participated in military operations led by JNA? Who commanded these municipal TO units and to whom they were answerable?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The absolute priority when it come it is to engaging units is given to a JNA unit or the largest unit participating in an operation. I've already explained you that. If the SUP unit is the largest one participating in the operation, it can have within its composition both the JNA and the TO units, but only if the SUP unit is the largest. In this case, the JNA via the president of the republic and president of the municipality resubordinates the TO unit. Once the operation is concluded, the TO unit goes back to its original location.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think you will have to clarify to the Judges what this "SUP" means.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secretariat of the Interior or the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is it the same as Ministry of the Interior, as MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So what is the difference?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ministry of the Interior has within its composition Secretariat of the Interior or SUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And when --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is called differently in different places.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And one last question. You mentioned many times today that you read certain information in press, in newspapers. What kind of newspapers did you read them? Was it Croatian, Bosnian, Serbian? What kind of place did you read it?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mostly read Croatian -- I mean, Serbian press. I didn't read Bosnian press, and I also read Croatian press which I received via Sombor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Milovancevic, there is -- there is a Prosecution motion -- I think it's Rule 89(F) or article 89(F) -- Rule 89(F), and I think the Defence has indicated that a response would be filed today. I just want to find out what the position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have prepared written reply, and we will give it to the Prosecution today. Otherwise, we do not object this motion of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On the 25th of January again the Prosecution filed a 92 bis motion. It looks like the Defence is supposed to file a response by no later than tomorrow. Do you have anything about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will comply within the deadline, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There is a question of dates here. I beg your pardon. Mr. Maksic, thank you so much. I should have asked you to -- I should have excused you some time back. You are excused. You don't need to come back to court any longer. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Bye-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm told -- I've got a note here that we have been given the 27th of February as a date we could sit, seeing that the Oric case is not sitting on that day. I'm seeing that for the first time, except that I already had -- had the 27th of February as a provisional date on my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: As did we, Your Honour. I thought that we had provisionally the 27th and the 28th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that March 1st we were not sitting, and then thereafter in March we were sitting every day is what I had understood. But certainly, with respect, the 27th and the 28th, I had understood we were tentatively set for those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, tentatively we were given those dates. Can I confirm with everybody that they would be available on that day. Would the Prosecution be available on that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the 28th?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the 28th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are also being asked to swap the afternoon sessions on both Tuesday, the 7th and 23rd. When I read the e-mail, I thought they said 7th and 23rd of February, now I see this note says 7th and 23rd of March. I remember making a mental note that today is in fact the 7th already anyway when I read the e-mail in the office. Is it March or February?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We didn't receive the e-mail, so I -- I can't say, but I would assume -- it sounds like it's March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, if it is March, what I don't understand is that we don't have a calendar for March yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, that's right. But I've been -- I've been told that we're sitting every day in March. And I think there is some calendar out there that exists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- that confirms that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're sitting every day in March. All they want is to swap?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's what it sounds like, and of course we would have no objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not quite clear from this note, but from my recollection from the reading of the e-mail, it looks like on those days we are scheduled to sit in the afternoon and the request is that we go -- we sit in the morning so that Krajisnik can sit in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's certainly fine for us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have the schedule in front of me now; however, we will comply with any instructions received by the Trial Chamber -- from the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we not able to see the schedule on the monitor, on the LiveNote?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry about all this. Apparently we are not getting the 28th in February. Okay. So it's only the 27th. And, yes, it is the 7th and 23rd of March I'm told, so if everybody is agreeable we will sit in the morning on the 7th and 23rd of March. Okay? Okay. Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just need to address the Court about the remainder of the week in terms of the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We were just thinking about that. Can you address us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, as my recollection, and I can be corrected if I'm wrong, but originally this week I think we were going to sit only Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday, and Wednesday was a late addition to the schedule. When it was added we decided, based on the earlier witnesses this witness actually would take a little longer and we would go into Wednesday, so rather than call another witness, we just preserved Wednesday to finish this witness. Obviously we have finished this witness now. What that means is we do not have a witness for tomorrow. Our next witness is available on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Which means we just can't sit tomorrow then. Then the matter then will have to stand postponed or adjourned until Thursday, the 9th, at 9.00 in the morning in this courtroom. Okay. The matter is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 9th day of February, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.
